utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Subotic. When we adjourned --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When we adjourned yesterday, we were discussing aspects of Srebrenica in 1995. I had -- you had mentioned or the issue of directives came up in the context of your statement. I mentioned that we would be turning to the question of directives, and so I wanted to turn to paragraphs 231 through 233 of your statement, and those paragraphs reflect a discussion about directive for further operations number 7 signed by the Supreme Commander in March of 1995 as we see in paragraph 231, and you explain in your statement that you learned about directive number 7 after it had been drafted. That we see at the beginning of paragraph 232. You describe that Dr. Karadzic went to the Main Staff, and as you say in paragraph 233, a few days after his return from the Main Staff I asked the president what was discussed. He told me it was about drafting and signing a directive and a large number of other documents. The paragraph goes on to describe how you reminded him that -- of your understanding or agreement that you would be present and review contents to which he replied, well, General, who am I supposed to trust if not the generals at the Main Staff, and then you state that the president would never knowingly put his signature under that disputable text of directive number 7. That's found at the last sentence of paragraph 233. First, General Subotic, what were you referring to when you indicated the "disputable text of directive number 7"?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I personally did not see the directive at all. I did not have it in my hands ever. However, later on before I testified in 2006, there was a dispute, as far as I understood it, and as I say, I have never seen the directive personally. As far as I know, there was a dispute about the sentence which allowed some use of force or something of that kind. To be honest, I would like you to quote from that directive, because I don't know. I have never learnt about that, which is why I claimed that. Because we had a system, President Karadzic and myself, according to which all the documents that were of some significance had to be reviewed. Otherwise, what would have been my role in the office? I was the expert, especially in terms of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You described that in your statement, and I referred to it just a few minutes ago. In fact, your statement contains an excerpt or two from the document itself at paragraph 231, there's a reference to the sentence as follows with reference to the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves "by planned and well thought-out combat operations create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." So as a matter of fact, you yourself refer to portions of that, and is that one -- is that part of the disputable text that you were referring to? In other words, were you -- were you saying in your statement that this is the kind of thing that you claim Dr. Karadzic would not knowingly have signed because of the nature of what that says, or are you referring to another part of the document?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I had in mind that part. I have not got the translation of paragraph 231 into Serbian, but now you have jogged my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, good. I would also call up 838, the document itself, and turn to B/C/S page 15 and you can see it. And that's also found on English page 10 in 838.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's on the screen, sir. You see under the Drina Corps in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You see the end of that first paragraph? "By planned and well thought-out combat operations --"

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "-- create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival --"

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "-- or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." And, sir, when you were calling it disputable --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- isn't it the case that what you meant was this is a patently illegal order to create no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of those enclaves?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely. Absolutely. I accept what you are saying. This is absolutely what was disputable for me. Knowing President Karadzic and what had been done by the two of us up to then, I have a serious doubt that President Karadzic ever read this. I don't know how things unfolded in the Main Staff. However, I doubt that he would have accepted this if he had read it. Moreover, now that I look at it and when I reflect on this, I may not be mistaken if I said that I believed that President Karadzic never read this, and on the other hand, I would not exclude the possibility that that page had been subsequently either altered or tempered with in another way. Because you see, you legal professionals, all the lawyers in the world initial all the pages of any serious document. I personally believe, or, rather, I doubt that President Karadzic ever read this. I don't know whether he read this, whether that was how it was written. I would not be able to say. So these are my serious doubts. However, knowing him --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you don't have to make the same point repeatedly. I understand your position on that. So it's your position -- let's set aside for the moment your speculation that somehow this was substituted afterwards, it was your position in your statement and as you just stated here that the Supreme Commander signed a directive that laid out the course of operations for his military forces after participating in the drafting of it without bothering to read it. That's your position. And that explains why Dr. Karadzic's signature is on this document that contains this order; correct? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What confuses me is this: The principle concerning strategic documents pertaining to the army was such that a document was prepared by the Main Staff. That was the first draft. The first draft was then discussed, and then possible corrections were made to that draft. If I had participated in the drafting of this document, I am giving you a serious guarantee that I would not have allowed this be written in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And apparently your testimony is that Dr. Karadzic is the kind of guy who when he gets a document that dictates what his forces will be doing doesn't bother to read it but says, Great, here's my signature. That's it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that he did not bother. I cannot say that. I wasn't there. If I had been there, I would have sat down together with Radovan Karadzic, I would have looked at the document together with him, I would have perused it together with him, and then I would alert his attention to a possible irregularities. I'm telling you this very honestly and I adhere that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what prevented you from looking at the document after it had been signed? Did you consider it to be the equivalent as a nonrefundable plane ticket?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not in the office -- or, rather, that document was not in my office. I did not have an occasion to see it. It was signed in Han Pijesak and that's where he stayed as far as I know. I personally never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you why you didn't ask to see it. I didn't have to -- why didn't you say to Dr. Karadzic, You know, I didn't a chance to review it, as you say you had agreed, so let me take a look at it and make sure there's nothing problematic, disputable, or more realistically illegal about it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement, and I said that I should have seen it. However, I don't know whether he was convinced that that's not how it was written. I don't know. What I stated in my statement is correct. I can't change it now. I can't speculate. However, I have my doubts about President Karadzic having allowed this to be said or written. These are my doubts, and I have to share them with you. And there's nothing else to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on to a somewhat different aspect of the operation and consequences of the operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question from me for the witness. I'm not sure whether the witness could assist us. Could we see the first page of this document in B/C/S. And the second page in English. General Subotic, this directive 7 is dated as 8th of March, 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the second last page in the B/C/S and the first page in the English. But the date on which General Milovanovic sent out this directive to the unit was 17th of March, almost ten days after the signature date. Can you tell us why it was so, if you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see here that the Main Staff of the VRS - and this is first time I see the document - sent this to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, and I don't know why it was sent to the 1st Krajina Corps. I wouldn't know that. Let me just read the two sentences here. I don't understand anything. I don't know why this was sent to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka in the first place. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's so natural that if a directive, some document like directive has been signed it should be circulated to the subordinate units, but is it usual to send or circulate this kind of document after almost ten days after the signature? Would it be usual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, in general terms, in principle I would not find it commonplace, but I don't know why they did that. To put it simply, I never saw this document, and I can't say anything concrete about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 185 of your statement, General Subotic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 185; right.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just bear with me, please. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You describe some issues raised around the beginning of October 1995 concerning the exchange of prisoners, first talking -- that is you and Dr. Karadzic, talking to Serbs who were interested in having prisoners exchanged and presumably therefore having Serbian prisoners come home, and then a conversation or -- or a discussion that Dr. Karadzic had apparently following that discussion with the representatives of the people who had been killed in Vijenac about exchange, Dr. Karadzic talking to the commission for exchange to try to arrange an exchange. So if I understand that correctly, after the conversation with these Serbian civilians who were concerned about the fate of their family members, Dr. Karadzic then contacted the commission for exchange and said get in touch with the Muslims and arrange for exchange. That's an accurate understanding of what you've -- the information you provided? That's just the backdrop to the question I want to ask you. So is that -- do we have an accurate grasp of the situation at that time? Talk to these people, they wanted an exchange, Dr. Karadzic then talked to the commission to assist those -- those concerns.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm very precisely and say that things happened as they are described in paragraph 185. I can't change any of that. I can read the paragraph for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, but I wouldn't change a single word in this paragraph. The conversation that happened that night had a huge impact on me. I'm very familiar with the situation, and I can only confirm that the veracity of what is written in paragraph 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And then the people he was talking to at the Commission for Exchange said where are the prisoners from Zepa and Srebrenica? And Dr. Karadzic said well, as far as he knew, they had been exchanged. That's what you say here; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the fact is, General Subotic, that there had been enormous pressure that began very shortly after the fall of the enclave for the Bosnian Serb authorities to identify where the missing Muslim men and boys were and to -- where they were held or what had happened to them. Isn't that right? Do you acknowledge that? The enormous pressure from the international community, and indeed even ultimately pressure from the Serbian community because exchanges weren't -- were -- of Serbs were being held up because of the question of where the men and boys from Srebrenica were?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept just the last part that you said, and the other thing remains as I said it. Because what is stated here by those people, by the parents, they are angry at Mladic and at others about why there was no exchange carried out between Zepa, meaning the Muslim prisoners and the Serb prisoners. What I wrote I cannot change, and I do not accept any other variations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, is it your testimony that you were unaware of any pressure from the international community, either the international media, or international representatives on the Bosnian Serb authorities, and particularly Dr. Karadzic, to identify where the thousands of missing Muslim men and boys were?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. No, not at all. I did not have any information, nor did I know, and it wasn't my area of responsibility either. There are other commissions. Others were entrusted with that. That was not something that I was entrusted with. I stand by this completely, behind everything that is written in paragraph 170 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I thought I understood you in the course of your statement to make a point about your concerns about the -- what the international media was saying; in fact, there's a portion in your statement devoted to propaganda and what the international media was saying about the Bosnian Serbs that you considered unfair. Let me give -- let me just recite for you quickly a little bit of the evidence in this Court about what was being written in the international media in the aftermath of Srebrenica. So at P4397, on the 17th of July, there was an article in the British publication "The Independent."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction as to the previous answer of the witness: It's paragraph 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That discusses a film that was made two days after Srebrenica and what it shows, a reference by a UN official to General Mladic reportedly saying that Serbs had been forced to kill lots of people because they were trying to break out of Srebrenica. The article says the fate of the menfolk of Srebrenica has been a concern to their families and international human rights since the enclave fell last Tuesday, and first a delegation of the ICRC being prohibited from visiting Bratunac where many of the captured Muslim men were believed to be held. Just a few days later P4398, referring to possibly the biggest mass execution of Muslim prisoners by the Bosnian Serbs in more than three years of war. According to residents of the Bosnian Serb controlled town of Bratunac and Serbs from Serbia who had visited the area, as many as 4.000 captured Muslim men from Srebrenica have been killed by the Bosnian Serbs. Two days after that, 4400, 23 July another article even if -- saying even if a fraction of the stories emerging from Srebrenica are true, the men of Zepa have every reason to be afraid of becoming POWs of General Mladic. And again referring to information from residents of the Serb controlled town of Bratunac and Serbs from Serbia about thousands of captured men from Srebrenica who had been summarily executed. And stories of mass executions of prisoners have started to cross the Drina River, irritating Bosnian Serb authorities because this time the tales are recounted by Serbs. Or just one more, P4401, two days after that reporting that in the days after Srebrenica fell, residents reported seeing truckloads of men being brought to shallow pits dug on the other side of the river bank and shot by Bosnian Serb soldiers, and stating -- and reporting that thousands of men from Srebrenica were taken prisoner by the Bosnian Serbs after the "liberation" of the Bosnian enclave on 11 July. Some estimates of prisoners executed are as high as 4.000. Now, is it your testimony, General, that none of this information and none of these allegations and none the concern of the international community reflected in these articles was known to you at the time, that you had no awareness of this whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that all of this is a lie. I would not assert that it was a lie had these gentlemen from England called Serbian journalists so that together at the actual location they could establish what the situation was, and then they could write the article together in English and in Serbian. Then I would believe them. I read six books about Srebrenica which were written after the war with all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've mentioned that [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is why I do not believe, I do not believe at all, Mr. Tieger, this. I didn't even know about this, this -- this title, nothing like that. I don't believe that. I just simply don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it been realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking for your opinion about the accuracy of these articles. We have a lot of information about that, General. I was asking you if you claim to have been totally unaware that these reports were being made and disseminated internationally.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state that I did not know that at all. I state that absolutely. Only after the end of the war I learned some other things. At that time, I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you unaware that on July 24th, 1995, the Special Rapporteur of the commission on human rights sent Dr. Karadzic a letter expressing his deepest - and I'm referring now to P6396 - expressing his deepest concern regarding the recent events in the Srebrenica area which resulted in the forced displacement of some 40.000 individuals and referring to reports that as a result of these events several thousand individuals are unaccounted for and there is fear that many have been killed or detained and calling for a proper investigation and evaluation, and in particular, calling for access to those who had been detained during the recent events? Were you unaware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know. I absolutely did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about a letter sent to Dr. Karadzic by the Special Representative for the Secretary-General on the 12th of August also requesting access to investigate these allegations and what happened to the men and boys of Srebrenica, to the thousands of men and boys who were the subject of the international community's concern. Were you unaware of that too? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity to see the letter or to know about it. I didn't have the opportunity. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you claim this is something Dr. Karadzic didn't mention to his special advisor. He kept this from you.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say that he did not mention it or that he concealed it from me. I don't know. Perhaps I wasn't there. I have no idea. I am simply not aware of it. I simply don't know about it. If there is a letter, this letter in Serbian, perhaps I could refresh my memory, but like this, no, I -- I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- could we have the exhibit number for that letter? I couldn't find it in e-court [overlapping speakers] by the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the 12th of August, letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 8 of the transcript, the witness did not say the -- the -- I would not say that he did not mention it or conceal it. This "did not mention it" is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. This letter has not been translated. I can read it to you. Dear -- it's dated the 12th of August, 1995. It's from the Special Representative the Secretary-General for the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Akashi. It states: Dear, Dr. Karadzic, it refers to the Resolution 1010 of 10 August in which the Security Council expressed its deep concern and reports of grave violations of international humanitarian law in and around Srebrenica and at the fact that many of the former inhabitants of Srebrenica are not accounted for. I am equally concerned at these reports, especially at the allegation of the existence of a mass grave identified by the government of the United States of America. And he requests as a matter of urgency and in accordance with the directives of the resolution he mentioned, that Dr. Karadzic allow UNPROFOR, and co-operate with UNPROFOR, to investigate the report of the existence of a mass grave and requests immediate access for representatives of UNHCR, the ICRC, and other international agencies to persons displaced from Srebrenica and Zepa in areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina under Bosnian Serb control. Then he asks further that ICRC representatives be permitted to visit and register any persons detained against their will, including any members of the forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I mention that to you as another reflection of the concern by the international community and pressures placed on the Bosnian Serb authorities. Is that a document again that you profess to be -- to have been completely unaware of reflecting concerns by the international community and demands by the international community that you also profess to be unaware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended practically all the meetings between Akashi and Mr. Karadzic, and I took notes, kept the minutes, and if any of this was referred to, then I am aware of it. And I knew that Mr. Akashi and Mr. Karadzic would always and frequently speak in Pale or in some other places, and I was always present, and I knew that. And this was talked about. All the questions were talked about. There was an understanding. There were agreements about these things that were happening, but this specific something that you offered here I did not take part in that, but I know that the president always allowed, as far as the Red Cross is concerned and UNPROFOR and as far as all the international organisations are concerned. He actually had problem with the army and the commanders, actually, because he always permitted everything that the international community asked to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So I'm a little confused now. Are you saying you were aware of these pressures or you were not aware of these pressures by the international community to allow to identify where the men and boys of Srebrenica were and to allow access to them if they were still alive?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the international community was pressuring Republika Srpska every minute, every moment, and you are asking me now to split hairs. I always was under pressure, not just myself but everybody in Republika Srpska. How could I have known about every instance of pressure by the international community? These pressures were there every day. So I will tell you what I know sincerely. I'm not afraid of anything. But don't impose any mention of any pressure on me that I'm not aware of it. There's no reason for that. I am not aware of this. Therefore, I cannot discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Subotic, you said you are not aware of this. You were not aware of this at the time. But do you agree that Mr. Karadzic received this letter from Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that he did. If you say so, then I believe that he did receive it, because I know that he had contacts very, very frequently and very solidly with Akashi. I don't have any doubts about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Karadzic had received this, you would also have received this as well. So is the thing that you now don't remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not receive the letter. I did not have the letter in my hands in the Serbian language. Therefore, had I had it, I don't know if he had received the letter, I would believe that he would have taken measures to do what Akashi was requesting in the letter. But this was not in my remit to deal with this. This was in the remit of other structures in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you -- this is one part I don't follow among your answer. You said: "I did not receive the letter. I did not have the letter in my hands in the Serbian language." When an international actor like Mr. Akashi, who was in particular the Special Representative for the Secretary-General, when they -- when such international actors sent that letter to Mr. Karadzic, did they send also in Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't know. I know mostly whenever I was at the talks with Mr. Akashi there was interpretation into Serbian. I would take notes. Ninety per cent of the conversations then I would note down. As for this specific case, we did not have, as far as I can remember, talks, because then I would remember it. I would have it written down somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You answered that you didn't have the letter in the Serbian language. It sounded to me that you received the letter in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I wanted to say was I would have known about it had the letter been in Serb. I would have known. Perhaps I didn't express myself properly. It's logical if I had seen the letter I would not have know what it was about because Karadzic did not give me the letter or speak to me about the letter. I don't know if I was at the office at that time. I don't recall simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Getting back to paragraph 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. There seems to have been an omission on the part of French translation. I take it it will be supplemented later on. Shall we continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in light of this backdrop, General Subotic, getting back to paragraph 185 where you state that Dr. Karadzic said that as far as he knew the prisoners from Zepa and Srebrenica had been exchanged, I want to ask you what you meant by -- what you understood he meant by "as far as he knew." So did -- how many prisoners did you understand had been exchanged, prisoners from Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The number of prisoners was not -- actually, you saw here that these parents were angry. They were asking where Mladic was and where Tolimir was and why were the prisoners from Zepa not exchanged for their prisoners. That's how I understood it in that conversation and that is what I noted down. Therefore, that is disputable. We didn't know Radovan or I when we spoke with them whether they were actually exchanged or not, but he said, As far as I know, the prisoners were exchanged. But we were not there. Other teams were there for the exchange of prisoners, but at that meeting there were just the two of us because the parents came to address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And according to you, what steps did you and Dr. Karadzic take in the wake of this meeting to find out whether or not prisoners from Srebrenica and Zepa had been exchanged, how many had been exchanged, and when that exchange had taken place?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any information prior to the meeting nor did we know that they would come. They came at midnight to the office in Banja Luka. At midnight, Mr. Tieger. We were just caught up, caught out in the situation, both Radovan and I, and then we asked for the people who were deal with that, who knew what was happening with the prisoners to come. The two of us didn't know anything about it. I mean, simply what I wrote down is what I stand by. I have nothing else to say regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And your testimony is that by October of 1995, there was no particular reason for you or Dr. Karadzic to have any awareness of where Srebrenica prisoners were or how many there were or whether they had been exchanged; correct? That's your testimony. So you were just caught out when this issue came up.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I want to turn to another subject, and that is something you raised in paragraphs 240 and 241 of your statement, and that's about Blagaj Japra, the Japra Valley, and in those paragraphs -- okay.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please see the text in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Subotic, this statement that I'm referring to was prepared by you and the Defence, or at least by -- I mean, I don't know the extent of your participation in this firsthand, but this is a document that has your signature on it and to which you attest -- yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can I please see the document so I can just remind myself. I cannot memorise so many pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What's in front of you right now? I see there's a document in front of you. What is it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see before me is in English. It states "Blagaj Japra," 240.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what's the document --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, what is the document that you have on the table in front of you if it's not your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a document on the table. Paragraph 240, page 91, Blagaj Japra, but it's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 241 is also in English, on page 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Subotic, there's only -- there's only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness. If you did not understand your statement, how could you sign the document as your statement? You confirmed that you signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a statement in Serbian, but it statement I didn't bring my own. I was told that I could not bring anything into the courtroom, but this is something that I found on the desk here, the statement, and it's in English. You have Serbian and English sporadically. I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you see the last page. Last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed. I signed the document, but I didn't know that in my document -- well, in my document everything is in the Serbian language, the document that I received from the Defence, but this one is partially in English and partially in Serbian. The paragraphs and the pagination are the same. I don't know why this happened. Perhaps it's because of something on your ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'll read out the passage where Mr. Karadzic asked you questions. It's yesterday's transcript, page 39984. Dr. Karadzic showed you the statement that you have with you now: "Do you see that statement of yours on the screen? "Yes. "Have you read that statement and have you signed it? "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read it in the Serbian language and I signed it, but this, this, theirs, I mean mine, the one I have in the hotel, all of it is in Serbian. I didn't even know that there is this mixed thing, Serbian-English. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we strike out the witness statement? I think probably Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson need to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe that the witness is mistaken. What is in front of him is what he signed, and what he signed is a compilation of his statement as he gave it to Mr. Sladojevic and also the excerpts from his verbatim testimony in the Krajisnik case. So that's what the statement consists of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is contained in paragraph 24 is part of his statement which he gave on 20th of May, 2006.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, having heard this clarification, are you minded to change your answer with regard to paragraph 240?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean change? I don't understand the question now. If I knew how to read this answer or if someone would read it out to me, then I could recognise it or not recognise it. But I don't know how to read it, so I don't know whether I can change it. I believe that that's it, but it's just written in the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask one question to Mr. Robinson for clarification. Take paragraph 240. That's a part of witness's statement. I take it there's a Serbian version of his witness statement, isn't it? Why do we have it English here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, Mr. Sladojevic has told me he's not sure actually what the status is of the portions of the statement that relate to interview by OTP of Mr. Subotic, so he believes that they may also have been in English like the Krajisnik testimony, but he's not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I'm concerned whether we need to strike out all the English part from his statement. If you could assist us in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. First, definitely with respect to the Krajisnik testimony, this is no different than other 92 ter witnesses who have listened to their testimony before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But we need to satisfy the requirement that if asked, witness would have answered the same question here. That's not satisfied here in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe he would say that if -- that his testimony he gave in the Krajisnik case was the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he wasn't offered that opportunity, because he can't read English at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's true, but he gave the testimony, and I also believe he listened to the recordings of the testimony from the Krajisnik case. So he can say that the answers that he gave would be the same, which is what I believe he has said when he was first questioned by Dr. Karadzic. So those portions that are in English from the Krajisnik case I think fall with the same parameters that we have for other witnesses who have testified in this Tribunal and whose testimony have come under 92 ter. With respect to the statement from the interview, we would have to check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation to make, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, just a couple. I mean, first of all, it is the case that witnesses in the past who cannot read English, instead of being shown a transcript had reviewed the previous testimony or the previous statement in another form so that they were in a position to affirm that that was accurate. So I don't have a problem with the modality, and I'm not trying to suggest that. And the -- and I'm not trying to make this particularly a precise memory game for the witness so that he has to be able to correlate the paragraph number with information he previously reviewed for the purpose of making the statement, but that's -- and, in fact, the -- the -- my point in raising this was not to challenge that the witness had said what he said - it is reflected in paragraphs 240 and 241 - but instead to point out what was omitted that he also said but didn't make it into the statement that appears in front of Your Honours. So I wasn't actually challenging the position that he didn't stand by 240 and 241. He's repeated several times, and I think he would -- whether he recalled what he said in Krajisnik or not, that he doesn't back down from that. But in this particular instance, it's a question of selective identification of what he previously said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether or not the Prosecution is challenging, I'm concerned about the requirements of Rule 92 ter have been met in this case. Did you try to say something, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have two variants. The first variant is that you allow me within 10 minutes of time to bring my own statement that I have at the hotel and everything will be fine. The second variant is that this be read out to me from English into Serbian, and I will immediately confirm whether that's it or whether it's not, and I will say what I know, but precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So by way of -- by way of example, let me turn to paragraph 241.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If somebody could read that out to me in Serbian, then I will answer Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will do that. This is pat of your testimony in Krajisnik case. So Judge Orie asked you: "Judge Orie: This Chamber received evidence which suggests that such an event did take place, and that is not just stories, but that includes documentary evidence, that includes some pictures. So, therefore, if you say, well, hardly could have taken place since we didn't know about such a massive event, I just inform you that of course there was no finding from the Chamber in that respect, but there is quite a bit of evidence." And you answered like this: "I have no reason to doubt what you're saying, but I do have reason to doubt that anybody in Pale was informed. I can simply not fathom that somebody could have been informed at Pale without raising a campaign on that issue. That's the only thing I'm saying." And this is my question for you: Before you signed the statement which is in front of you, did anybody of the Defence team read out that paragraph to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They read that part out to me, and they gave it to me in the Serbian language in my copy of the statement. I don't know. I didn't go into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Subotic. I would like you to be precise. If you don't remember, please say you don't remember. You said that the Defence team gave this part in the Serbian language. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. It's not that it was given to me. It was read out to me. But I was told that this would be -- I mean, in my copy in the Serbian language, all of it, not only this, but also those other ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Be precise, please. Did you receive this part in Serbian language, or the Defence team only read out the part to you? Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- well, they had two copies. I didn't know that in their copy this was in the English language. I received a copy in the Serbian language. All the items, all the paragraphs, all the pages. I have that copy, but since I was told that I'm not allowed to bring anything into the courtroom, I didn't bring that, but I have a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Subotic. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, His Honour just kindly read out to you what 241 says, and that's the gist of what you convey in your -- the information you provide about events in the Japra Valley and the awareness in Pale and among the Bosnian Serb leadership about what happened; that is, that you have reason to doubt that anybody in Pale was informed because nobody raised a campaign on that issue. Now, that did not reflect the entirety of the discussion that took place during your testimony in the Krajisnik case, and if we turn to pages 26470 --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- I mean, I don't understand this question sufficiently. What I said in the Krajisnik case, well, I wasn't asked for anything precise. I wasn't asked for anything precise. I was just -- I mean, well, the statement I gave is what I knew then. It's not that I had any precise information and so on, and no one asked me for precise information. But later when the statement was taken from me, I mean in 2012, that was something different because there was information that was accessible to me and that was generally accessible, a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what you said in the Krajisnik case to Judge Orie was that: "You see, Mr. President, this involves," and again this is referring to the Japra Valley operations, "... this involves a huge amount of people, 4.000 people. It's not a small group. It's neither 4 nor 40. I believe that there is nor municipal authority or police force in that area that could have kept this from the government or Pale. Since that was never a subject of discussion ever, I simply cannot conceive that something like that could have happened without anybody having been informed whereas the communication lines were working." So what's not contained in paragraphs 240 and 241 is the fact -- is your position that there is no way that this event, that any municipal authority or police force from that area could have kept this information from the republic-level authorities or from Pale; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. I stand by that and that is what is written in my statement, the one in the Serbian language, likewise what Mr. Tieger read out just now. And I stand by that and I cannot claim anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to another event not involving 4.000 people but involving a large number of people that was known -- also known to the authorities in Pale, and that's the events at Koricanske Stijene. And that's referred to in your statement at paragraphs 242 through 260. And in those paragraphs, Mr. Subotic, you relate the awareness of Dr. Karadzic about the event, refer to a session of the Presidency or at least the attendance of Presidency members and others at an ad hoc meeting or session, Dr. Karadzic giving you the order - and at this time you were the minister of defence - giving you the order to go to Banja Luka and hold a meeting. Your participation in a meeting involving prosecutors, judges, chiefs of police stations in the area and others, and passing on verbally the order of the president and the Presidency to take immediate investigative actions and all actions necessary, et cetera. And then it also provides information in the subsequent paragraphs about some of the -- about what happened afterwards and what transpired. For example, you were asked the question, it appears in paragraph 244, how many of those policemen who escorted or guarded the convoy were interviewed about what happened to what, as it turned out, were more than 200 Muslim civilians who were massacred. And you indicated you didn't know, you were not informed about that. So that's the event in the portion of your testimony that I'm referring to, Mr. Subotic. Now, as part of your statement, you indicate that one -- you suggest there that there were three people responsible for the killings at Koricanske Stijene, that is three policemen, one of whom was prosecuted, two of whom were killed, presumably meaning in combat after they fled, after they went to the army. First of all, when you refer to one person prosecuted, you're referring to one person prosecuted many years later by the ICTY and convicted of that crime here; right? Or do you claim to be aware of somebody else who was prosecuted by Republika Srpska authorities for the murder at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I gave that statement in the Krajisnik case very precisely and in great detail, and in that statement I said all the things that I learned at that meeting in Banja Luka, when this entire team went to the site, to the scene of this crime, where we visually saw this area. So I gave this statement only on the basis of the notes I took at that meeting. What I was told by the police, the judges, in order to be able to convey all of that to the state Presidency. That was my task. Everything that you repeated just now about those three persons, I noted all of that down at that meeting in Banja Luka. That is to say I -- actually, that is what I was told. I was not an investigator. I was not aware of the case. Quite simply, I conveyed the information to the Presidency. I know, I do know, later when the trial took place and so on, that it was, after all, the way you are saying. It wasn't only these three, and so on and so forth, but I could not judge anything, I could not investigate, and that is why my statement -- I mean, I claim that it's only from that meeting and that event where we were on that day, nothing else. And I personally condemned that at that meeting, personally, as a human being, and I asked absolutely for very precise investigations, and so on and so forth. So I have nothing else to say with regard to that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, this is not exactly a major whodunit. Everybody there knew that the people who had been killed were part of a convoy that was escorted by a policeman from the Prijedor Police Station; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, probably you turned off your microphone. The interpreters did not hear you. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying -- I mean, I don't know which part I should repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat all over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my task was in Banja Luka at the Ministry of the Interior to bring together all relevant persons and institutions that should explain to me what it was that had happened. The president, who entrusted me with this task, or, rather, the member of the Presidency were primarily interested in the following: Whether the military, the army took part in this. Immediately at the beginning of the meeting that was eliminated. The army had nothing to do with that event. So it was the police from Prijedor, and all of it was explained to me. I wrote all of that down precisely, who said what. The head of one centre, the other centre, and everybody else who took part, I explained all of that when I testified at Mr. Orie's. I did not know whether it was true or whether it was not true, whether that is exactly the way things happened or not. Later on in the later period I found out because that was made public. There were trials, arrests, and so on. What Mr. Tieger said to me just now, that was confirmed exactly, but I didn't know about that. I could not inform the Presidency about that because the information I provided was what I wrote down specifically. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you said just said that according to you you eliminated from the outset that it was the army and knew that it was the police from Prijedor. That was the question I had asked you. So policemen had been sent to escort the convoy, which means that -- that since you had the police chief -- the relevant police chiefs there, everybody knew who those police member were; right? Right there on the spot, their identities were easy to identify.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, they just announced three persons to me, I mean as an answer that I could convey to the Presidency. I don't know anything else. Whether they did know or whether they did not know, that was their affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're suggesting that this matter was considered so important by the leadership that it sent you out personally to make sure to order that all appropriate measures were undertaken to solve it. I'm saying to you it was crystal clear who was involved. Do you even know if any of those people were interviewed, interviewed, by Republika Srpska authorities in connection with this crime in 1992 or 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about later when I left. I know that the ministry took part, the MUP, and the Ministry of Justice. As I said, there were judges, and I don't know all the relevant ones, but I didn't take part in that. Did I not have an opportunity to learn about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has received evidence that the people involved and responsible, directly responsible, hands on, for these killings were not in hiding and had anyone been looking for them they would have been found. And you can turn to P4257 for that evidence. And that makes sense, doesn't it, I mean, since their identities were known as policemen, it wouldn't have been so difficult to get ahold of if anyone had wanted to find them; right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have that, I believe that's the way it is, but I do not know about that, but, say, logically I can infer that these persons should know that if, as I said, they said that later. Well -- but I was not in the know. Had I known about that, I would have conveyed that immediately, and I would have included it in my note.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so that would further suggest that people involved didn't want to find them. That also logically follows, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what you are claiming, this would be a logical conclusion. However, I cannot claim that because I didn't participate in any of that. That was not my task. It was a task that was supposed to be carried out by investigators, judges, prosecutors. I don't know who else, but in any case, professionals. I was not at the receiving end of any further information. I didn't receive any information, and I didn't really express any interest in receiving further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So according to you, these most elementary aspects, the most rudimentary aspects of a serious investigation were not undertaken, but you didn't care, and as far as you know, I take it, Dr. Karadzic didn't do anything about it or care about it either?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we had zillions of other problems. We had institutions that were in charge of those matters. It was not up to the two of us to monitor the work of the police, the formers [as interpreted] of everybody else and their uncle. You have to understand that we are not computers. Competent people were tasked with doing that. Whether they did it or not, I don't know. I know practically nothing about what they did. However, that was our system. So the system had to function, and things had to be done according to that system. I cannot invent things in order to satisfy somebody's needs or requirements. I don't know. How was I supposed to know what the police did? I was not the chief of the police or the minister of police, for that matter. I knew for a fact that the military did not take part, and that was what mattered to me. And the rest I did according to the Presidency's instructions. I submitted my report. The ministry did their own job. The prosecutors, the judges did what they were supposed to do, and I don't know what they did. I did not get involved, therefore I cannot discuss that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Last question before the break. Slobodan Avlijas, the deputy minister of justice or at least a high ranking official in the Ministry of Justice at that time, participated in the meetings concerning what to do about Koricanske Stijene. That is the meeting in Banja Luka attended by senior officials, including you. That's T35186. And he testified and told this Court that everybody knew what had happened and that in any properly functioning state, Simo Drljaca would have been arrested right there. Do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I noted. What I noted I conveyed at the trial of with Mr. Orie. And as for that word, Simo Drljaca was removed from his position, so I don't know. I suppose that what you're saying is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca became an assistant minister in the MUP, a higher ranking position, and in fact was given a major award by Dr. Karadzic after this event, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was decorated because of that. Dr. Karadzic did not explain why people were decorated. It was the chiefs and commanders who were supposed to provide their input as to whether somebody deserved to be decorated or not. This is how things are done all over the world, in all the states. That's how people are decorated. And people can deceive a president, people can deceive a king, because things are not double checked; because if things were checked then no decoration would serve any purpose. I'm telling you this as an expert as the chief of a body in the Republika Srpska government. But look here, there is a law on decorations, and in the law on decorations it says that anybody who commits a crime or a big transgression, any decoration is taken away from them. I am the author of that law. I don't know whether this was really followed through if -- whether Simo Drljaca was decorated and whether the decoration was taken away from him. If he was decorated, then the chief of police, his boss, had to take the decoration from him because the law on decorations is a public instrument, and I don't know whether that was ever done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the record, decoration is found at P4261. I see we're overdue for the break, so that I will resume afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would request that the witness be allowed during the break to go to his hotel which is nearby to bring the version that he has of the statement so he can look at it and we could verify what it is that he has. I think he could do that within the 30 minutes of our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with it. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 10 past 11.00. I'm sorry. We'll resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a note, Mr. President, before I resume that I understand the witness brought the statement back from the hotel room. I considered that in the interests of time I might ask to take a look at it before the Court resumed the Bench, but when we began to do so, the witness was very interested in explaining something about it, so we just said, Stop, wait until the court resumes and anything that needs to be explained can be handled then. Mr. Robinson was with me, and I believe a representative of the Registrar as well. So that's where we are now. The witness has that document. I -- I haven't seen it. I know the Court inquired about it. Mr. Robinson raised it. It's difficult to know exactly in whose court this immediately falls, figuratively, but I presume the Bench wants to either ask about it or see it, and I certainly would like to see it at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to the parties. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Subotic, I understand that you went back to your hotel room, came back with the document, the Serbian version of the statement that you referred to earlier and you have it with you now. I would ask if with the assistance of the Registrar if I could briefly examine that document.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I provide a certain explanation for the benefit of the Presiding Judge? There was some confusion, indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have an opportunity to explain that, but at this time could you kindly provide that to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I understood you to stay, and I'm referring back to page 25 or 26 of the -- of today's -- of the transcript of today's testimony that you had two -- there were two copies. You didn't know theirs was in the English language. You received a copy in the Serbian language, all the items, all the paragraphs, all the pages. I have that copy, but since you were told not to bring anything to the courtroom you didn't bring it but you have a copy. Is this document that was just handed to me the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was my mistake. I was mistaken. If I may be allowed to explain in very simple terms. Can I explain things to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so far I have provided three statements to The Hague Tribunal, in 2007, 2008, and in 2006. All the statements have been translated into Serbian. I have received them, and I have them in Banja Luka, and I have initialed all the pages in those statements, and those statements are in Serbian, exclusively in Serbian. That's why I was sure that I have a statement in Serbian. However, when Messers. from the Defence took a statement from me, they were reading sections in English, and they asked me -- at the same time I had my own copies which were translated, and that's why I thought that those were valid statements, and I adhere by that all the time, because I initialed every page, and now that I have arrived here to testify, they showed me all that. I initialed everything, and this is theirs, their signature as well as mine. But I believed -- or, rather, I simply forgot. Otherwise, I would have told you that I had that translation. In other words, in that sense I suggest that when you're putting questions to me to read everything in Serbian and then I will confirm what I stated. I can confirm, because everything has been initialed. Well, this was my mistake. I apologise to the Trial Chamber and to you for having been convinced that I had that in my hotel. I don't. I did not bring of that. I did not dare take those statements with me on my travel. This is what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to make this clear, because I'm not sure that your explanation was completely clear to the Court, when you said you were mistaken, this document I have in front of me now that you brought back from the hotel room is a mixture of English and Serbian; right? So some paragraphs in English, some paragraphs in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those paragraphs which were taken from my previous evidence given before The Hague Tribunal, only those paragraphs. I suppose that the Defence did not have them translated into translation, whereas I do have all that translated into Serbian, because after each time I provided evidence I received the translation of the evidence into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, I am not aware that your -- that the testimony you gave in the Krajisnik case was transcribed into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it in Banja Luka. I received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who do you say transcribed that and provided it to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was the office in Banja Luka. This was done subsequently. And as for what happened in Pale, I received that personally in Pale, those two days in Pale. Since I was in Banja Luka on several occasions in that office, I believe that I received it from them. In any case, I got it from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you say you have a copy of your Krajisnik testimony in the Serbian language in Banja Luka that you can provide us.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can send it to you from Banja Luka. I don't know how, but I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can make arrangements for that. Meanwhile let me return this document to you for such use as you may make of it with the -- with any portions that are in Serbian that may be referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to round out this topic, I would like to just inform the Chamber that we -- I have an e-mail here where we requested the transcript of -- the portions of the statement that were in English be transcribed -- be translated into Serbian but the language section declined to do that. So that's why, at least for our side of it, the statement was in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The version of statement the witness signed was in the B/C/S in most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He signed the version that's uploaded into e-court as the B/C/S original, which contains B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But his original statement was translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. His original statement was taken -- was -- his original statement is the one that he has in front of him. It was then translated into English by the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. I mean his statement of, for example, 20th of May, 2006, was it not translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was not translated. It was in English that we had, as far as we were working with the English, and so it was contained in English in the version that we considered to be the original version, along with the Krajisnik transcript references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have his statement with you? Paragraph 240, footnote 250, it refers to 65 ter 20639, witness statement dated 20th of May, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I understand it, we were working with English version at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you could have inserted this part into B/C/S, which was sent to the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, apparently that's correct. There are four statements as Mr. Sladojevic has explained to me. That's the only one that's in Serbian. And that could have been done but it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when witness said that he had all the statements in B/C/S version which he initialed every page, I understood in that way that -- so 240 could have been put in B/C/S, but I will leave it at that. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just on the heels of Mr. Robinson's comment, just to note that the information that CLSS declined to translate, the Krajisnik testimony is consistent with my understanding that there is no B/C/S version of that testimony, but I'll move on as the Court has suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, at paragraphs 219 through 226, you deal with the subject as the header indicates, "Prisoners of war and collection centres." And on the heels of our discussion before the adjournment about matters about which the Bosnian Serb authorities in Pale were informed, I want to talk about the information you provided in the statement and the information that was available at the time. Now, first of all, included in that portion of your statement is a colloquy between Judge Orie and yourself during the Krajisnik testimony when Judge Orie quoted to you from a record of the government session held on the 15th of June, 1992, which stated: "'The government has considered the proposed report. It has been concluded that the issue of prisoner exchange is extremely important, complex, and delicate, and that if sufficient attention is not paid to it, it can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic. It has been agreed that a working group consisting of Professor Branko Djeric,'" who was, as we know, the president of the government at the time, the prime minister, "'Milan Trbojevic,'" who was the vice-prime minister, "'Dr. Dragan Kalanic,'" minister of health, "'Mico Stanisic,'" minister of the interior, "'Bogdan Subotic,'" you, the minister of defence, "'and Momcilo Mandic,'" the minister of justice, and it provided they "'should consider all the aspects of the prisoner exchange problem and they should propose systematic and other solutions, taking into account our international regulations. It is obvious that solving this problem is urgent and that the regulations and concrete measures for solving this issue should be proposed as soon as possible.'" And you indicated to Judge Orie you -- that this was a reference to prisoners who had been taken, you said, on both sides of the municipality. Prior to that -- although you emphasised that these were prisoners taken on a local scale and not major battles. Now, Mr. Subotic, the language that accompanied the establishment of this working group, referring to the problem as important, complex and delicate, that's a reflection, is it not, of the awareness at that time that thousands of Muslims and Muslim civilians in particular had been taken under detention and if that problem wasn't resolved there would be significant -- could be or would be significant negative consequences for the Bosnian Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear at that session that thousands were mentioned. I didn't hear anybody mentioning any figure. And as for the rest, I accept that, but no figures were mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, did you -- when -- when you came to understand, as reflected in the report, that the problem was extremely important and complex and required the involvement of the highest officials of the government, including, as mentioned, the prime minister himself, the vice-prime minister, the minister of the interior, and so on, did you make any effort to find out the extent and scope of the problem?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us and for me personally it didn't make any difference whether we were talking about three, five, a hundred, or a thousand. It was all the same to me. As far as I can remember, and I didn't note any such thing, that any figures were mentioned. It's different if different places. This was based on different information. In any case, that problem was very seriously taken into account, and this is how things were done at the time as far as I know during the first government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you had an opportunity during the course of your Krajisnik case to see a photograph of at least some of the people who had been held in custody, and you acknowledged, and it's there in your statement in paragraph 226, that it was "... illegal, to hold people in detention and treat them in a fashion that resulted in a condition like that" depicted in the photograph; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not quite like that. You remember very well if you read everything what I -- you were also present in the courtroom. You remember very well that I said things were staged, and I showed how some images, some photographs, were not adequate. I explained a lot of that to you. You are aware of that, so I don't see any need to discuss that. I entirely stand by my statement of that day. I have nothing new to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So is that your testimony to this Trial Chamber, that you are not aware of -- or you did not acknowledge in any way that prisoners were held in Bosnian Serb detention facilities in condition that reduced them to an emaciated condition, that were not held in unhygienic [sic] conditions, under -- with -- with inadequate food? You're denying all that and saying it was staged, is that it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I stand by my statement absolutely, and if you wish, because the Trial Chamber and all the people present here would need to hear my statement and then decide on it. I stand by my statement, and I have nothing further to add, the one that I provided to Orie. I cannot, otherwise that is that. I have no other statement. But -- and I cannot give you a different answer, because you did not read to the Trial Chamber all that I said in the statement. I would like the Defence and the others to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what it is. I could read it out. If I had a Serbian translation here, I would read it out. I would ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to read it out. I have no other answer for you other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm asking you a question in front of this Trial Chamber, in front of these Judges right here, and I'm asking you if your position is that Muslim -- Muslims were held in Bosnian Serb detention facilities and treated in a fashion that resulted in their near starvation, that -- that they were held in conditions where hygienic facilities were totally lacking. Basically they were held in brutal and inhumane conditions. Do you -- do you accept that that was the case, do you deny that that was the case, or do you say that you don't know? What is it as you're testifying before these Judges now?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that I did not give such a statement the way you are telling it now. I provided a different statement, and I stand by that statement that I provided to Mr. Orie. And you are asking me in a suggestive way for me to accuse somebody or defend somebody in a way, and that's something that I cannot do. What I said in that statement stands before this Court and the court of God, and I have nothing more to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, one of the things you acknowledge in that statement, Mr. Subotic, is that you were the person responsible for providing -- for ensuring that soldiers had sufficient food and supplies - that's at page 26533 - correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which soldiers? Whose soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As minister of defence, were you or were you not responsible for ensuring that the VRS had adequate supplies, ammunition, food, and so on, or was that not part of your portfolio?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, yes. I was. That's true, but it's not the way you are telling it. It's different. Read exactly what I said, exactly what I said, please. Please do not impose things in a leading way. I do not accept that. I did not say it the way you are telling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Question at page 26533: "Q. What was in your domain, Mr. Subotic, according to what you told us, was logistics including such things was food; right? "A. Yes."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Just specifically -- all right. Yes. Yes. And it is still a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who do you claim was responsible for providing food to the prisoners taken and held by the members of the army for whose supply of food you were responsible for?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know who was responsible. I don't know who was responsible. I don't know who that was. You did not ask me that there, and I did not give an answer to that then. You're asking me now that now, and I don't know to tell you who it was. I was not the head of any camp or a quartermaster in order to be able to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact -- in fact, you said in your testimony it was the responsibility of whoever set up the camp to ensure that the prisoners were fed, and that's at page 26523.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger, read to me -- read to me word-for-word what I said. Then I will give you an answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, when this working group was set up about the complex and delicate and extremely important problem of prisoners, did you or anybody else make -- on that working group make an effort to find out how many prisoners there were and how they were being treated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was done, but I don't have any indicators now, because I took the least part in that, so I didn't have any numbers or anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see a camp, actually, for myself, with my very own eyes. I just saw it on television or something like that. I did not see it in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you denying that there were thousands of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat prisoners being held at that time, civilian prisoners being held at that time, or do you say that you don't know or that it was true?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any figures at my disposal. I personally have no figures available, and I'm not able to say anything with any certainty, because that's not something that I knew, and I didn't have any possibility of knowing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You had no possibility of knowing it, Mr. Subotic? The -- on the 1st of June, 1992, the 1 KK sent a report to the Main Staff, that's P5398, about the 7.000 prisoners they captured during events around Prijedor. On the 17th of July, 1992, a report was sent to Dr. Karadzic and to Professor Djeric from the Ministry of the Interior stating: "The army, Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible, and they leave them -- leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs.
