The conditions in some of these camps are poor. There is to food. Individuals sometimes do not observe international norms, et cetera." At the 17th Assembly session -- and that by the way was P1096. At the 17th Assembly session held on July 24th to 26th, 1992, Representative Milanovic stood up and said - and that's at page 30 through 31 of the English and page 30 of the B/C/s: "We have a huge problem with captured people of other nationalities. We have hundreds and thousands of these prisoners." On the 2nd of June, 1992, a day after the VRS -- the -- the report from the 1 KK to the Main Staff I referred to earlier, Dr. Karadzic met with Radislav Brdjanin - and that's according to as we see in P1478, at pages 55 through 61 - and Brdjanin talked about the problem of the Krajina with 14.500 Muslims and wanted a position about prisoners from the highest level. Now, in light of that information plus more, do you seriously assert to this Court that you had no possibility of knowing that thousands of Bosnian Muslim and Croat civilians were being held by the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You don't deny that was the case. You just say you weren't aware of it; is that it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not denying anything, not do I know that it was like that, and I don't -- this report was not something that I had in front of me. I'm seeing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence, Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I repeat the last sentence? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did not know and that I don't know and that I was not aware either of this report or of the figures, and I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've got a limited amount of time left, so I want to move on to just a couple of more topics, Mr. Subotic. At paragraph 26 of your statement, you say the Serbs made no -- "there was no plan. Serbs did not make any plans before the war." Then you go on to say that only the Muslims made plans. Now, this Court has received evidence that Dr. Karadzic talked both before and after about the steps that he had formulated and was prepared to take. For example, P1387, English pages 74 through 75, B/C/S pages 57 through 58, at the 38th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, Dr. Karadzic recalled the earlier days, and he explained how all the steps were carefully planned to be executed once at a time, and he said: "Let us use Alija's mistake to increase the price of wine. Remember how all the SAOs," that's Serbian autonomous regions, "and all those measures before the war always took place following Alija's mistakes. There were nine to ten actions that we carried out. We brainstormed them all together. However, we did not pull all nine moves straight away, but we carried them out after Alija made a mistake. It is then we'd make a move and the Muslims would curse his mother afterwards and not ours." And similarly in P2554 at a SFRY Presidency meeting in December 1991, well before the 38th session, Dr. Karadzic again explained: "We made a list of moves, ten moves in the direction that we want that the result be. But we do not put them into action until Alija Izetbegovic messes something up. When Alija messes something up, we make move number five and then we wait, and when he messes something else up we make move number six." And said the same thing in P953 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's break it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So is it your position that Dr. Karadzic never told you, despite the fact that he told everybody in the Bosnian Serb Assembly and everybody present at the SFRY meeting in December 1991 that he had plans for what was going to happen in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such contacts with Mr. Karadzic in 1991. I didn't know him, and I didn't even know he existed. Specifically, in this case, I have no ideas about that. This is something that I never -- I'm hearing of this from you for the first time, so I cannot give any comments on this. We can move on. Let's go to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about one of those very concrete steps that were taken. You referred in paragraphs 52 through 55 to Crisis Staffs, and tried to assert to the Court, did assert to the Court that they were all self-organised and had nothing to do with the Bosnian Serb leadership; right? That was your position?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this Court has heard a lot of evidence about the document commonly known as Variant A and B, which called for the establishment of Crisis Staffs. For example, P2568. We heard from a member of the Main Board and Executive Board about his presence at a meeting of SDS functionaries at the Holiday Inn during which Mr. Karadzic distributed numbered copies of the Variant A and B document to municipal representatives and gave a speech about the threat that Serbs were under, and their municipal leaders were called up to take the Variant A and B document. That's something you didn't know about, Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. In 1991, I did not have any information along those lines, and I did not act along those lines. I was doing some other things in 1991 to prevent the attack of Croatia on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have a lot of statements about that. As for this, I don't know anything about this. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's move to 1992. For example, on January 26th 1992, at the 6th Assembly session of the -- of Bosnian Serb Republic, in front of the Assembly, during which there was a discussion about the further steps that the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats had taken toward a sovereign and independent Bosnia, Mr. Cizmovic stood up and said: To resolve this problem I propose that we begin with an urgent operationalisation and a declaration on the establishment and promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out. And then this Trial Chamber has heard repeated evidence that on the 14th of February, at an extended session of the Main and Executive Boards, including municipal presidents and so on, Dr. Karadzic activated the second level of variant A and B in a speech that referred to that second level four separate times, including saying that's why we called you here today. You didn't know about that either?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know any of that. I began to acquire knowledge on the 8th of April, 1992, when I came to Pale. Before that, I never went to Pale, and I did not contact anyone. So I have no information or any other evidence that I know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just tell you about -- you refer to one -- two Assembly sessions you were present at where this information was brought to your attention in a very explicit manner. First the 46th Assembly session, that's P1403, and then we're talk about the 50th which we talked about before. So at the 46th Assembly section at English pages 347 through 348 and B/C/S 304 --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of that, please? Could you please say it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll get that for you in a second. I thought I had it. That was November 1994, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me which paragraph, what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm also telling you that the transcript of that session, which is in evidence, also reflects your presence at the session. But more importantly, here's what Dr. Karadzic said at that session and then said at the 50th: Everything was as clear as day in the municipalities. He said, Please, remember how we used to work before the war. Everything was as clear as day in the municipalities where we were majority and in those where we were minority. Do you remember the instruction A and instruction B? We had Crisis Staffs, and it was clear they were the authority. They could make mistakes, but they were still the authority. The people were not left without the authority because they were the Crisis Staffs. And then at the 50th Assembly session to which you've explicitly referred in your statement, Dr. Karadzic said the following - that's P970 at English pages 316 to through 317, B/C/S page 278: "At the moment the war began in the municipalities where we were in the majority we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, Municipal Boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You will remember the Variant A and B variants. In the B variant where we were in the minority, 20 per cent, 15 per cent, we had set up a government and a brigade, a unit, no matter what size, but there was a detachment with a commander. Distribution of weapons was carried out thanks to the JNA. What could be withdrawn was withdrawn and distributed to the people in the Serbian areas but it was the SDS which organised the people and created the army. It was an army. Together with the people, those were the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They created the space, liberated and created the space." Mr. Subotic, those are words by Dr. Karadzic spoken in your presence that clearly indicated the plans that were set in place and implemented by the Bosnian Serb authorities before the war contrary to your assertion in your statement that there were no plans by the Bosnian Serbs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have those plans? Could you provide those plans so that I can see them? I cannot understand that you can say this from I don't know where. Do you have the plans of the Bosnian Muslims? Do you have the plan of the Serbs in order to be able to assert this before the Trial Chamber? You cannot just be talking off the top of your head. Crisis Staffs existed. All of that existed, but these were necessary, a necessary evil. And of course we organised ourselves in some fashion, but you don't have any documents that were not legal. Show any illegal document on the basis of which Republika Srpska was established and then we can talk and allow anyone, let anyone, anyone from Bosnia and Herzegovina, give you such a plan, a copy. We cannot just be talking off the top of our heads, Mr. Tieger. These are just leading things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suggest we not talk off the top of our heads. Look at paragraph 26 of your statement, please, and tell me if you didn't testify before this Court in the form of this statement that, "Serbs did not make any plans before the war"? Is that your testimony or not?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see. Let's look at paragraph 26. It's in the English language. Please read it out for me, and then I'll see when I did or did not. Read it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "There was no plan. Serbs did not make any plans before the war." That's a direct quote from the signed statement.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did not make any plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I just have one more topic to cover with you, sir, in the limited time I have, and that's in relation to the document that Dr. Karadzic showed you yesterday. That's 11274. During which he -- this is a session of the Bosnian Presidency during which he took your attention -- drew your attention to a portion of that document that referred to the declaration of a state of war, and he asked you: "Did we declare a war on the Muslim-Croat coalition? Did they declare a war on us?" And then you were shown that document. Now, I'd like to show you other parts of that document just to identify the context in which that declaration of war was discussed, and if we can call up 11274, please. If we can look at page 1 of the English translation and page 24 of the B/C/S moving on to 25. That's a reflection of Mr. Halilovic talking, and he's talking about indications about agreement of exchange and resettlement, and then he talks about playing directly into the hands of those whose intention it is to create some ethnic territories, to move the population, and to create national units. Turning to page 2 of the English and page 25 of the Serbian -- or B/C/S, we see Mr. Abdic talking, who expresses concern about the need to talk more about the fact that UNPROFOR has been put into a situation where ethnic cleansing is being carried out under its supervision. Page 3 of the English, page 28 of the B/C/S, Mr. Izetbegovic says: If we don't accept the ultimatum, these people really could be hurt. utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it's date? I cannot see the date here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May 27th 1993.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 27th of May, 1993. This is the first time I see this and hear of it, but I know what this is about. So it is well known that the first conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina occurred in Prijedor, the first one as far as the Bosnian Krajina is concerned. I wouldn't dare speak about Herzegovina and the rest down there, because I'm not familiar with that. This conflict occurred already in the beginning of May in Prijedor, and during that time I was minister in the Government of Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say I came on the 5th -- on the 8th of April. After that I assumed my duty, and, I don't know, for more than a month, I think, I did not move from Pale at all. Since communications were very bad at the time, we had not even established a government yet in full. There were five or six of us. So that is to say that the formation of the government was underway. Some information was coming in about clashes between Serbs and Muslims, ethnic groups in the town of Prijedor itself. Now, what happened there and is to what extent, we did not know. We were not in a position, we from the government, not at all. We hadn't even been established yet as such for -- for us to get any meaningful information. Time elapsed. Sometime in 1993, in the month of May, Haris Silajdzic, in a public statement on the radio said that in Prijedor, in the beginning of May 1992, 5- to 7.000 Muslims were killed. Around the 12th of May - I'm not sure. I don't remember correctly - in 2003, among other things, I became the chief inspector of the army. I personally heard this information in Pale. And that was the first time I heard of anything like that. Then I decided, because that was my task, to check because I knew it wasn't the army. In Prijedor, in May, there was the JNA, a military unit, but it was in Slavonia. As far as I remember, it was precisely in Slavonia. So in this conflict with the Muslim population or fighters or whatever, I don't know how it was that they clashed, it was the Territorial Defence that took part. It only could have been the Territorial Defence, possibly the police. That is why I, around the 22nd or 23rd of May, I cannot remember exactly, I went to Banja Luka. I asked for information as to what it was that happened in Prijedor in May, what Haris Silajdzic had stated in the media. It turned out that no one could tell me anything specific, and I addressed precisely this Colonel Bogojevic who was head of security in the 1st Krajina Corps, and I asked him and he said, We don't know all of it either, but the Prijedor police would have to know and the Territorial Defence. They were the ones who took part in this. I asked the colonel that we go there and see. We found Colonel Arsic there who was commander of the JNA unit who maybe could have or should have had some information about that. I, Bogojevic, and Arsic went together to the police to see Drljaca, who was chief of police at the time. I don't know exactly what his exact title was. I first put this question: Did the army take part in this? The explanation I was given was that this military unit, I think it was called the 27th or some brigade, that was a JNA unit, that it was somewhere in Okucani or towards Papuk, but that that was this clash between the opposing parties, that is to say the Muslims and the Territorial Defence in Prijedor. Simo Drljaca, well, I asked where were these people who were killed buried, and he said at the mine of Tomasica. I asked that we all go there together to see whether anything can be seen there or something like that, because according to military regulations in a state of war, and so on, which had already been regulated, well, not exactly in May but by the end of June I as minister of defence issued these regulations. This was regulating how this should be done, how people should be buried, one's own soldiers, enemy soldiers, and so on and so forth. I asked that we take a look, and when we arrived there, so that is about a year after this massacre, I asked Mr. Drljaca. He said that it was the materials that took part in this and part of the police. I asked how many were there, because I said Haris Silajdzic -- well, this is what initiated my interest in it. When I asked the question how many people, fighters, or whoever they were, civilians, were buried there, he said up to 500, up to 500. I could not make any decision then. For me it was important that the army didn't do it, and that was confirmed by Colonel Arsic and Drljaca. When actually after that Krajisnik and I went to see the president of the municipality we talked a bit about that, but he said that's how they were buried. That's how it was. No one touched anything. The location and time are well known. When I returned to Pale, I notified the minister of justice, it was Mr. Jovo Rosic, and I asked him, I mean I explained this to him, what it was that I found out, and I asked him to start an investigation about this case. What happened after that I don't know. That is what I know about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One follow-up question. So your testimony is that before the attack on Kozarac on May 24th, 1992, before the confinement of thousands of Muslims and Croats in Omarska and Keraterm, before the room 3 massacre where 150 people were killed, before the attack on the Brdo in July of 1992, before the killing of over 150 people from the Brdo and Omarska and so on, that already at least 500 and according to Bogojevic, 5.000 Muslims had been killed before that in Prijedor? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we were told by Drljaca to me, Bogojevic and Arsic. I didn't know anything about that, to be honest, although there were rumours. There was information that we received in Pale that there had been conflicts between Muslims and Serbs in the territory of Prijedor. There was nothing strange about that. The war had already started, therefore there was nothing specific. And as for Kozarac and the rest, I really at that time -- I did not have a possibility or time to deal with that problem at all throughout the entire first war -- year of the war I didn't have the time, or at least up to June I didn't. Perhaps two or three times I turned up in Banja Luka and once I was there with Krajisnik. When we went to visit the president of the municipality, I know that Krajisnik asked him about the situation with the population in Prijedor, and that was sometime around the 12th or the 13th of May. He said we have about 5.000 Muslims, about 5- to 6.000 Croats in terms of the other population. That's what I know. I remember that very well. After that case, in 1993 I remember that, and then I wondered how come that there were 5.000 Muslims and that they were killed by the Territorial Defence at the beginning of the war since the Territorial Defence perhaps had one company. I don't know how many. I didn't know how many men they had at their disposal. So who was it who was capable of killing that many people? I didn't find any of that logical. But listen, see, according to Haris Silajdzic there were 5- to 7.000 and so on and so forth. In any war the figures get exaggerated, and that was also true of Srebrenica and so on and so forth. This is what I know about that case. I don't know where this has come from, where this information has come from. From Bogojevic? I haven't a clue really. I really don't -- am surprised. What did he say? Let me see. Just bear with me for a moment. That Subotic got involved. What does that mean? What does it mean when he says that I got involved? What was I involved in? Maybe he thought that I as the main inspector of the army and I came to check the situation. I don't know what I was involved in. As a minister, what was I supposed to be involved in during the first days of the war. I was in Pale. I didn't know whether I was coming or going, what was I supposed to do, how I was supposed to set up my ministry from the 12th of May onwards? I really don't understand. He should explain his own words to you, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to that burial and sanitization, did that happen before or after you issued your instructions?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were buried immediately after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. This is the second time Dr. Karadzic is introducing terms of art that have particular connotations that were not either -- they're not contained in the document, for example. Now we have sanitization. Previously we had casualties. It's clear what he's intending to convey with his use of the words, and I want to urge open-ended questions that don't direct the witness to particular formulations of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what instructions did you give in the month of June after the army started functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prescribed everything in terms of documents concerning warfare, the burial of casualties, and so on and so forth. Therefore, I didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That provision concerning burials, what does it set out? Which casualties is the army supposed to bury?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from some parts, for example, in Zvornik where I was present when General Stankovic, who is a pathologist, dealt with some casualties in Zvornik that were buried at the cemetery, and they were Muslims. Pathologists did their bit that they were supposed to do. They had documents. The graves were marked with numbers. I saw that, and that was in accordance with the military regulations that prevailed in the JNA and in all the other militaries in the world. I had an occasion to see that. That was prescribed by our rules and regulations. People could not be buried in any way. Their graves had to be marked. Their names had to be known, and so on and so forth. And later on the mortal remains could be transferred to other places depending on requirements and some other thing. I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was every killed enemy soldier buried in the place where they were found? What procedure was followed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, it depended on the conditions. For example; I don't know why those people in Prijedor did it the way they did. In Prijedor there are Muslim cemeteries and so on and so forth, so they could bury them in Muslim cemeteries, which would have only been fair, and so on and so forth. They should have marked those graves. However, maybe the conditions were not in place. Maybe it was not possible due to fighting and conflicts. I don't know. I never investigated the circumstances. My information dated from one year after the conflict and after the burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, after the war or at any time, were those bodies exhumed when that burial site was discovered? Did anybody mention the number of bodies that were found there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from the media, from the press, and from TV that that burial site in the Omarska mine was exhumed. To be honest, I was never in those mines, so I don't know what the name refers to. However, that information did not contain the number of casualties, but that was done after the war. I know that. In peacetime I don't know when, in what year, but that can be checked in the territory of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked whether you denied that Omarska, Keraterm were camps where the civilians and fighters were detained and other people. Can you tell us how many people were released from Omarska and Keraterm and how many were found as guilty of having participated in fighting?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that I had even before the end of the war, 60 per cent of the people who were detained there were released. I don't know what happened to the remaining 40 per cent. I don't know. I'm not privy to that information, but I know for a fact that I came across information according to which 60 per cent were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was it who was in charge of the investigations and triages that happened there? Who was it who decided that some should be released and that some should be kept? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: More of the same and I'm going to keep rising when this keeps happening. You can scour the transcript. There is no mention of triage up to now. This is part of a continuing pattern by Dr. Karadzic trying to indicate to witnesses where he wants them to go and what assumptions he wants them to build into their answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I don't agree with that. This is not a leading question and the witness is free to give any answer he wants. I don't think that Dr. Karadzic is asking an improper question at all in this way. I don't really understand the basis for an objection that Dr. Karadzic is creating some kind of suggestion to the witness. The question is open-ended. He can answer it in any way he wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the word "triage"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, that's not suggested. It's up to -- if that's how Dr. Karadzic characterises and the witness understands what the import of the question is that's not suggestive simply charactering of something one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In my system, as Mr. Robinson well knows -- first of all, we should be arguing this outside the presence of the witness, but never mind. This assumes facts not in evidence. So Dr. Karadzic wants to ask the witness about something that the witness has not testified to, that was not raised in the examination, that is now presented as a fact and ask him who was in charge of that fact that the witness hasn't testified about and that wasn't part of any earlier answer. That is the existence of triage. Now, and -- and as I said before, this is another reflection of the same pattern that exists of providing the witness with something as a fact and then having the witness automatically build it into his answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, these 60 per cent, were they released --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Bear that in mind. The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger's observation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, according to what you heard and found out these 60 per cent, were they just released indiscriminately, and what about these other per cent and what is this the result of? Did others decide about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others were aware of that. I didn't know about it, but nobody asked me about it. Mr. Orie didn't ask me about that. I was responding only to Mr. Orie's questions. I didn't know who would be asking me what. So this means that the investigative organs interviewed individuals. This was publicly shown by the organs of power. It's not a secret. All those who were not -- who were not -- who did not participate in the fighting, and so on and so forth, who did not, they were released. I know that for sure. There's nothing else to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move to page 54 of today's transcript where the declaration of war was discussed. First, I'm asking you this: It was read how I said that the municipalities had their own units. Are you able to tell us whether the municipality has the right to any armed formations and to which ones?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law on the national defence of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the municipality had all the powers in that sense at the municipal level. This is particularly interesting until the formation of Republika Srpska -- or, rather, for the beginning of the war, until we formed our own organs, laws, and so on and so forth. So we copied certain things from those laws. We did not change the laws of Yugoslavia. Therefore, the municipalities did have such powers at the municipal level. They had their own Municipal Staffs. They had their own weaponry. They had -- all of this existed on one side and the other side, the Muslim side, the Serb side, and the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked or actually what was disputed was your assertion in the testimony in the Krajisnik case that Serbs did not have any preparations. What sort of preparations did you mean when you said that you did not have any preparations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs had no preparations at all for armed fighting. They simply had -- Serbs had political preparations, preparations through which they attempted, and it wasn't just the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina but in Croatia, Slovenia, and so on and so forth. They were trying to convince people not to go into war, not to embark on war, that if we needed to split up then we should split up. So that was it. No Serb was willing to participate in the war. Not a single Serb. Believe me, we loved Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia was a wonderful country. Therefore there were no military preparations that were carried out until the beginning of the war. As one says only with the entrance of the army to Sarajevo, they were escaping in front of the enemy, they were getting killed in Sarajevo. It was then that people understood what it was all about, how things were proceeding and then they began something at their own level, they made some attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then my learned friend Mr. Tieger said as I -- that I said that we had a series of pre-planned moves. When Mr. Izetbegovic made one move, we made another move. So this political counter game, did that lead to war? Did it have a military nature?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was just precisely that political game that tried by all means. This is generally known. Everybody knows this. Muslims in Sarajevo know this, and many Muslims would confirm that, and -- and they could testify to it. Thus no one was in favour of war. Quite the contrary. We accepted that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be Bosnia and Herzegovina. It should be one state, because Yugoslavia was dismembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I'm going to keep objecting to this. So this is another example so Dr. Karadzic says to the witness about this matter. So did these political counter moves and so on. What the witness actually said when he was presented with that information was, I didn't have any contacts with Mr. Karadzic in 1991. I didn't know him. I didn't know he existed, specifically in this case. I have no ideas about that. Well, now Mr. Karadzic gave him some ideas and it comes out in his testimony and that's what's happening over and over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I also agree, and also it reduces the probative value of the witness's answer. While the Chamber is able to recognise such -- such the probative value of such questioning, but please refrain from putting a leading nature in your -- in your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I just wanted to respond briefly to Mr. Tieger. This was a consequence of the fact that Mr. Tieger presented our political measures to the witness as military, war measures, and that brought him into the situation of having to say that he didn't know anything about it. Had he read which measures we had taken, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is you that inserted the term political counter-gain and it's not appropriate when you conduct re-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, your Excellency, but in that case I would ask that the witness be shown the measures to which Mr. Tieger alluded so that we can see. He presented them as part of preparations for war, but they were not of a military nature, so he confused the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. It's up to you how to conduct your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just give me a little time to collect myself and I will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were shown the transcript of the 20th of June, 1992, where the Muslim side -- or, rather, the Presidency declares war and proclaims a state of war. Was this the first time that they undertook and adopted some aggressive warmongering actions in relation to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They already from the attack by Croatia to -- and preparations for the attack on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is this the first time that they adopted some aggressive warmongering actions in relation to the Serbs? Please reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time that any law was being referred to or mentioned which would direct towards fighting against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. Already from the beginning, after the formation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the referendum, this already started to be prepared and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at D332 in e-court, please. General, sir, please, could you read the date and the first sentence and then could you read paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of National Defence, Territorial Defence Staff, Sarajevo, number such and such. The date, 20 -- I don't know if this is 20 -- 20th or the 27th - I'm not sure - of April, 1992. Order on the implementation of decision number such and such of the RBiH Presidency pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you read item four now?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four: Hurriedly plan and begin combat operations in the whole territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and co-ordinate them with the Territorial Defence staffs of regions, districts, and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In planning combat operations, plan extensive measures of protection of the civilian population and property of the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Commander Colonel Efendic. Hasan. I'm missing some letters, but last name is Efendic. This is the person who replaced Vukosavljevic, General Vukosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, against whom should combat actions be planned and commenced on the territory of the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not against angels or anyone. It's against Serbs and probably Croats at that time. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please remember, Mr. Subotic, to put a pause before you start answering the question. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serb side at that time or at any point later did it make a plan and issue a similar directive for offensives on the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or in territories which were majority Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not ever until perhaps the end of 1992 when there were orders by the army for certain operations like that, but otherwise before that this was not definitely the case, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see 1D44050 in e-court, please. There is no translation, but I'm briefly just going to read five or six lines. First of all, let's identify the document though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're about to see a document that doesn't have an English translation, so I won't be able to tell why it's being raised at this point to this witness, but -- so I'm a little bit lost as to the manner in which this arises from the cross-examination and what is intended by putting this particular document in front of the witness rather than seeking whatever information he might have that's relevant to redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, there was a question as to the declaration of war and the conduct and actions of the Muslim army and possible preparations on the Serb side. The topic is the same as the one dealt with with the previous document, and the author is the same, General Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's not justification for leading the witness, which is apparently what this is an effort to do. Meanwhile this document is in front of the witness and he's reading it. So Dr. Karadzic, as has been his custom, one way or another continues to try to lead witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He put a question, albeit very brief, on the previous page. Very well. Now that the witness has read the document, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he didn't read the part that I'm interested in. It's on a different ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this directive correct, General, sir, is this how they acted based on this directive from the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that situation. First of all, I would like to tell the Trial Chamber that in Bosnia and Herzegovina this post was health by General Vukosavljevic, and he was replaced because he is a Serb by ethnicity even though he was married to a Muslim woman from Sarajevo. Therefore, he was not suitable for the preparations, because he wouldn't do that. He was lieutenant-general by rank. He was a very serious man. I knew him personally. We all knew him, because he was the commander of the Territorial Defence for the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina for a number of years. So he was deliberately replaced so that Hasan Efendic could subordinate himself to Alija Izetbegovic and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he could be acting according to the wishes of Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to put a document to the witness, first you should put a foundational question and lead the witness to tell us what this document is about, and you may then proceed to ask some content of the document. I don't see from the document what this directive is about at all, and I don't know what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, the directive has been taken down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Just wait. The directive has been taken down. I already put questions on it, then it was adopted. This is D332 it was earlier on the screen. This is a review by the same man about the development of the military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence. Put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. General, do you see this document? Can you tell us what the document deals with?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is justifying the declaration of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather, Alija's declaration of war, and he is trying in some way to explain that, the reasons for declaring war. That is the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see page 4. What is written there? Can you read out the heading for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I have page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please have the first page yet again and could you read it out.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Development and growth of defensive liberation forces." Please, this is clear. Defensive liberation forces. These are forces that were attacked, not those that are defending themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic, what you were asked about is to read out the title. Please concentrate on answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I agree with the Court's guidance, and I also think it's clear that what's happening is that in lieu of asking this witness focused questions that might elicit information that he has in a non-leading way that arise from the cross-examination, instead he's being turned to documents that Dr. Karadzic wants information to be elicited about and being asked to read it out and affirm -- it's classical leading. It's also very peripheral to the cross-examination which dealt with the matter that Dr. Karadzic raised in a very specific way and now he's returning using that subject as a broad platform from which to discuss everything about Muslim preparations for war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll withdraw that, Excellency. I'm going to abandon this topic altogether and I'm going to go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, and I take it my colleagues would agree with me but I tend to agree with Mr. Tieger's observation. So, Mr. Robinson, if you could have a word with Mr. Karadzic how to conduct his re-examination in the future. Shall we adjourn for today with the witness -- with this witness and I will hear from the parties about Zametica's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed that we can -- Mr. Salapura's evidence has not been concluded which he will continue tomorrow for about half an hour or an hour. Yes. Mr. Subotic, you may be excused. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think I can shortcut this discussion just by doing some math here. I don't think we'll reach Mr. Zametica tomorrow, so instead I think we'll reschedule his testimony for the 3rd of July and that will obviate any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I certainly haven't thought through the impact -- what I understand Mr. Robinson to be saying is that the circumstances are such that he's in a position to reformulate the schedule in a manner that doesn't implicate any loss of time to the Court or any impact on the Prosecution. I actually haven't thought it through from that respect, but if his point is he can do something unilaterally that doesn't have any implications to the Prosecution's schedule, I suppose that's a way of saying it doesn't really matter what the Prosecution says in response. I haven't thought it through fully from that point of view and to see what impact it has, so my position was predicated upon the impact of dealing with that statement under the circumstances that we expected to occur, and you'd have to give me just about at least two minutes to consider the implications of what Mr. Robinson just suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Tieger. So we'll deal with it when it will arise as a matter of fact. So we'll deal with it immediately before Mr. Zametica is due to testify. There's one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask the parties whether -- or how they view this: Mr. Salapura is going to testify in the Mladic case tomorrow morning for some time, after which he's due to come to this courtroom and to give testimony, this time as a Defence witness. In terms of perception or appearance, whether there's any problem or whatever, can I hear from the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't see any problem. Maybe I'm missing something that is not blatantly obvious to me, but in reality, the Prosecution is interested in proving the events in Srebrenica and some of the things that occurred there, and they're using Colonel Salapura to do that in the Mladic case. We're interested in showing that Dr. Karadzic didn't have any knowledge of those events, and we're using Colonel Salapura in our case for that purpose. So I don't see any inconsistency, but if I'm missing something about the perception, maybe you can let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm also happy to focus on particular concerns the Court might have, but my initial reaction is that this is a reflection of an aspect of witness testimony that we see reflected in various ways when insider witnesses are called, and that is in part that parties may call witnesses in respect of particular information and ask the Court to consider the witness's testimony in light of the totality of evidence and the extent to which that witness's testimony about certain matters is convincing and credible and corroborated by the totality of the evidence and disregard other aspects of the witness's testimony that may be, for whatever reason, whether it's -- well, for various reasons, not considered reliable by the Court. So I -- given the position that certainly has been taken in respect of insider testimony in other instances, I think it would not be necessarily surprising that a witness's evidence is of interest in some respects to either party, although all of the evidence that that witness may provide may not be accepted or indeed may be challenged by the party that calls the witness, and I say that completely in the abstract, because I haven't conducted myself the particular analysis of what evidence I think the Defence specifically intends to rely on, what evidence I think is likely to be adduced from this witness in the Mladic case, but I think that broad principle is -- is one that we're familiar with in the institution. Given the fact that people close to the events are also people close to the -- very often to the accused and are other parties of interest, there is often a viewed need to elicit information from those people, understanding the possibility that not all information elicited will -- can be assessed in and given precisely the same weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In conclusion, you do not see it problematic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can say this, Mr. President, when you raise it, it makes me rethink it and -- and consider the possibility of -- of giving it further thought, but the -- the answer to your question at this moment is no, it is not something that we had intended to raise with the Court in the manner you just asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe there's some English custom that Mr. Tieger and I are missing, but we're going under the principle that the witness is not the property of either party and therefore it could be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't think you're missing any English customs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You're not, you're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think the Chamber's just acting out of an abundance of caution. But I speak purely for myself, if neither party sees any difficulty, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: This is the point. I mean, if both sides agree, then the matter comes to an end, but from the standpoint of perception, I thought that instinctively it might not have been the best course of action and possibly a day to interpose himself between the two bodies of testimony, but if both sides agree, then, you know, so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think especially under the circumstances where we wouldn't have any other witnesses tomorrow if we did have this problem, a gap, so I think it's better to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, I have exercised restraint, but this is not the first time that Mr. Tieger is mentioning that witnesses are close to me. Mr. Tieger called all the witnesses who are not close to me. And none of these witnesses that are called by the Defence are particularly close to me. Simply they are not Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of June, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
